name: Question 10
problem:
Express $z=\frac{3}{1-\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$
worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $1+\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3}{1-\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{{1}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{3(1+\text{i})}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\,\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{9}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $y=\frac{3}{2}$ are both positive, $z$ lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\frac{3}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})).
$$

First, we express the given complex number in the form z=x+yi. To do this, we remove i from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of z by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is 1+i: z=31−i=3(1+i)(1−i)(1+i)=3(1+i)12−i2=3(1+i)1+1=3(1+i)2=32+32i

In polar form, r represents the magnitude |z|. For a complex number z=x+yi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=x2+y2.

So, for z=32+32i, the magnitude is r=|z|=(32)2+(32)2=94+94=92=32=322.

In polar form, θ represents the argument arg⁡(z). Since x=32 and y=32 are both positive, z lies in the first quadrant. So, we can find θ as follows: θ=arg⁡(z)=arctan⁡(yx)=arctan⁡(3232)=arctan⁡(1)=π4

Finally, we write the complex number z in polar form: z=322(cos⁡(π4)+isin⁡(π4)).
